tweets.text:
Contrary to popular perception, most people will not adopt a new technology just because it makes them more efficient.

Instead, they’ll adopt new technology because:
- Someone they know who’s similar to them on some dimension adopted the technology, and got positive results (eg became cooler, richer, more popular/respected), and they wanna become like that person 
- They feel like everyone around them has adopted the technology, and if they don’t, they’ll be left behind

Notice that it’s not entirely a rational decision. It’s more of an EMOTIONAL decision.

So if you’re trying to make someone adopt a new technology, the messaging shouldn’t be “this will make you 10x more efficient!” It should be “So-and-so, someone you can relate to, has adopted this and look how much better their life has become; wouldn’t it be nice to be like them?”

This book reminds you of that. It can be distilled in one sentence: “The diffusion of technology is a SOCIAL process”

The best AI training isn't a course. It's pulling an agent into your team's group chat & letting people watch it work

tweets.text:
"LongCat Sparse Attention: Taming the Lightning via Streaming-aware Hierarchical Cross-Layer Indexing"

LongCat Sparse Attention makes sparse attention more practical at million-token scale by fixing the indexer bottleneck.

Other than just better indexing, they also made indexing cheaper, reusable across layers, and friendlier to memory access.

The result is near full-attention quality at 69B to 560B scale, with native 1M-token training for LongCat-2.0.

Read more about it here:
https://t.co/tZLTsZcZV3

"DiffusionGemma Technical Report"

DiffusionGemma turns Gemma 4 26B A4B into a discrete diffusion model that denoises 256 tokens in parallel, reaching about 20 tokens per forward pass and 1,500 tok/s on one H100.

By using SFT to teach bidirectional denoising, then use sampler distillation plus RL to reduce denoising steps, they did not have to train this DiffusionLM from scratch while maintaining generation quality.

tweets.text:
Ok builders, here’s your playbook. 

Prototype your product with the best frontier model. Cost be damned. 
Validate the user experience.

Then, 6-8 weeks later when open-weight models catch up - move your production workloads there, and to smaller models where possible.

In that order. Don’t start with the cheapest model.

The best model for early product validation is almost never the best model for production.

Talked to a bunch of founders this weekend. There’s a standard playbook emerging :

1/ Prototype with the best frontier models. Max quality. Ignore cost and latency.
Learn what users actually want and iterate. 

2/ Once the workflow and UX is validated, optimize like crazy for cost and latency - prompt eng, model routing, harnesses, smaller models, fine tuning. 

I see most teams get stuck in step 1.

tweets.text:
One fun benefit of spending so much time with enterprises is you get to see the array of AI implementation strategies that exist in companies right now. 

Unlike the early innings of cloud where there were really only a couple deployment patterns available -including being limited by only a couple infra vendors existing- AI actually has a much wider range of approaches in the enterprise.

If you ask 10 IT leaders what their coding agent strategy looks like, you get at least 5 different answers. If you ask about their end-user productivity agents, some have standardized on ChatGPT or Claude, others offer a choice of multiple solutions, and many have built their own orchestration layers for employees to use any model. 

For models, we know the big ones, but increasingly enterprises are experimenting with OSS models, or are at least immensely curious about OSS and would jump at the right offering that felt safe. And increasingly there’s a set of vertical models and agents that equally show up in enterprises for a range of tailored use-cases.

For accessing data, some enterprises just have agents take on the role of the user, and others are setting up agent users that have their own identities. Some companies are setting up substantial guardrails on what agents can do, and others are putting responsibility on the user.

Given this heterogeneity this early on at the start, it means we’re in for years of landscape changes. Anyone who’s predicting ultimate market outcomes already probably will be wrong as nothing has formally settled in yet. Lots of opportunity ahead.

Another day another near frontier open weights model release. 

If you had gone back even 3-6 months and given everyone access to what we’re now seeing in open weights even as a closed model, their minds would be completely blown. The fact that this is possible changes the calculations in the industry meaningfully. 

It means that models can’t reasonably remain behind closed doors for too long since there will be open weights models as a counter balance. It means AI inference will have to get closer and closer to the cost of the underlying infrastructure since you can always run open models yourself. 

It means that you get models that can develop in a range of industries for specific domain problems and not be held back by large training runs, which means more breakthrouhs in more spaces. And it means that more economics can spread between the model layer applied AI layer over time.

Incredibly exciting times.
